'''James Alexander''' "'''Sandy'''" '''Green''' [[Royal Society|FRS]] (26 February 1926{{Sndash}}7 April 2014) was a mathematician and professor at the Mathematics Institute at the [[University of Warwick]], who worked in the field of [[representation theory]].

==Early life==
Sandy Green was born in February 1926 in [[Rochester, New York|Rochester]], [[New York state|New York]], but moved to [[Toronto]] with his emigrant [[Scottish people|Scottish]] parents later that year. The family returned to Britain in May 1935 when his father, Frederick C. Green, took up the [[Drapers Professor of French|Drapers Professorship of French]] at the [[University of Cambridge]].

==Education==
Green was educated at [[the Perse School]], Cambridge. He won a scholarship to the [[University of St Andrews]] and matriculated aged 16 in 1942. He took an ordinary BSc in 1944, and then, after scientific service in the war, was awarded a BSc Honours in 1947. He gained his PhD at [[St John's College, Cambridge]] in 1951, under the supervision of [[Philip Hall]] and [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]].<ref>J. A. Green (1951) ''Abstract Algebra and Semigroups'', PhD thesis, [[University of Cambridge]]</ref><ref>{{citation | last=Green | first= James A. | title=On the structure of semigroups | zbl=0043.25601 | journal=Ann. Math. |series=2 | volume=54 | pages=163–172 | year=1951 | issue= 1 | doi=10.2307/1969317 | jstor= 1969317 | hdl= 10338.dmlcz/100067}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last2=Roseblade | first2=J. E. | last3=Thompson | first3=John G. |author3-link=John G. Thompson | last1=Green | first1=J. A. | title=Obituary: Philip Hall | doi=10.1112/blms/16.6.603 | mr=758133 | year=1984 | journal=[[The Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]] | issn=0024-6093 | volume=16 | issue=6 | pages=603–626}}</ref>

==Career==

===World War II===
In the summer of 1944, he was conscripted for national scientific service at the age of eighteen, and was assigned to work at [[Bletchley Park]], where he acted as a [[computer (occupation)|human computer]] carrying out calculations in Hut F, the "Newmanry", a department led by [[Max Newman]], which used special-purpose [[Colossus computer]]s to assist in breaking German naval codes.<ref name=mactutor>{{mactutor|id=Green_Sandy|title=James Alexander Green}}</ref>

===Academic work===
His first lecturing post (1950) was at the [[Victoria University of Manchester|University of Manchester]], where Newman was his Head of department. In 1964 he became a Reader at the [[University of Sussex]], and then in 1965 was appointed as a professor at the newly formed Mathematics Institute at [[Warwick University]], where he led the algebra group.<ref name=mactutor/> He spent several periods as a visiting academic in the United States, beginning with a year at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] in 1960–61, as well as similar visits to universities in France, Germany and Portugal. After retiring from Warwick he became a member of the faculty and Professor Emeritus at the [[Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford|Mathematics Institute]] of the University of Oxford, in whose meetings he participated actively.<ref name=donkin/>

==Work in mathematics==
According to the Fields Medallist [[John G. Thompson]],<ref>{{citation|author=Thompson, John G.|title=Vertices and sources|journal=Journal of Algebra|volume=6|issue=1|year=1967|pages=1–6|doi=10.1016/0021-8693(67)90009-9 |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82813217.pdf}}</ref> Green showed, in two important papers,<ref>{{citation|doi=10.1007/BF01558601 |title=On the indecomposable representations of a finite group |date=1958 |last1=Green |first1=J. A. |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |volume=70 |pages=430–445 }}</ref><ref>{{citation|doi=10.1007/BF01193108 |title=Blocks of modular representations |date=1962 |last1=Green |first1=J. A. |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |volume=79 |pages=100–115 }}</ref> that information about finite groups can be derived from knowledge about indecomposable modules of [[p-group|''p''-group]]s.

Green found all the [[character theory|character]]s of [[general linear group]]s over [[finite field]]s (Green 1955) and invented the Green correspondence in [[modular representation theory]]. Both [[Deligne–Lusztig theory|Green functions]] in the [[group representation|representation theory]] of [[groups of Lie type]] and [[Green's relations]] in the area of [[semigroup]]s are named after him. His final publication (2007) was a revised and augmented edition of his 1980 work, ''Polynomial Representations of GL(n)''.

==Personal life==
Green met his wife, Margaret Lord, at Bletchley Park, where she worked as a Colossus operator, also in the Newmanry section (Hut F). The couple married in August 1950, and had two daughters and a son.<ref name=mactutor/>

==Honours==
He was elected to the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1968 and the [[Royal Society]] in 1987<ref name=lmsobit>{{citation | url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/sites/lms.ac.uk/files/files/June%202014.pdf | title=Obituaries: James Alexander (Sandy) Green | magazine=Newsletter of the London Mathematical Society|date=June 2014|page=29 }}</ref> and was awarded two [[London Mathematical Society]] prizes: the [[Berwick Prizes|Senior Berwick Prize]] in 1984<ref>{{citation| url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Societies/LMSBerwick.html | title=Berwick prizes | publisher=The MacTutor History of Mathematics archive }}</ref> and the [[de Morgan Medal]] in 2001.<ref name=lmsobit/><ref name=donkin>{{citation|last1=Donkin|first1=Stephen|last2=Erdmann|first2=Karin|date=2019-12-30|title=James Alexander Green. 26 February 1926 – 7 April 2014|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=67|pages=173–190|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2019.0012|doi-access=free}}</ref>
